title: Leonardo da Vinci's Life In Reverse | From a French Chateau to a Tuscan Village
description:
Leonardo da Vinci's life is told backwards in this episode, beginning with his death at the manor of Cloux near Amboise in 1519 and rewinding to his birth near the Tuscan town of Vinci in 1452. The journey steps through the Roman years, the Last Supper in Milan, the abandoned clay horse, the engineer's map of Imola and the Florence workshop where he ground pigment as a boy. Every scene moves to an earlier date, so the paintings, machines and notebooks arrive in reverse order and the pattern of a working life becomes visible. Dates, places and commissions follow the documented record, and the later legends are named as legends.

scenes.narration: Today the most visited painting in the Louvre hangs behind glass in a climate controlled room, and it is the work of a man who never finished most of what he promised. Around seven thousand pages of his notebooks survive, written from right to left in his own mirror hand, full of machines, rivers, birds and numbers.

Five centuries before that, on May 2, 1519, Leonardo da Vinci died at the manor house of Cloux, just outside the royal chateau of Amboise in France. He was sixty-seven years old. His bones were laid in the chapel of Saint-Hubert at Amboise. A later story says the king himself held his head at the end, but that tale is disputed.

In the weeks before he died he drew up his will. He left manuscripts, instruments and papers to his pupil Francesco Melzi, and money to the servant and pupil Salai, who had come to the workshop as a boy. He also provided for the townspeople around him. The notebooks he valued most were the ones he never meant to publish.

Two years before that, in 1517, a cardinal's travelling party visited him at Cloux. The secretary of the group kept a diary and noted that the master was now old and that one arm had grown weak, so he could no longer paint much. He showed them pictures kept in a locked room, and they admired what they saw.

Three years before that, in 1516, he had left Italy for France at the invitation of King Francis the First. The king gave him the manor house of Cloux, a pension, and the title of painter, architect and mechanic to the court. He arrived with his notebooks, his pupils, and three pictures, among them the Mona Lisa and the Saint John.

Four years earlier, between 1513 and 1515, he had been living and working in Rome, in apartments near the Belvedere court of the Vatican, under the protection of Giuliano de Medici, brother of the pope. He painted the Saint John the Baptist and a Saint Anne, and he spent his money on a workshop of assistants, pigments and assistants again.

Seven years earlier, around 1510, he had been dissecting bodies in the north of Italy with the help of an anatomy professor from Pavia. Over the following years he filled notebooks with drawings of hearts, limbs and muscles, marking the valves and the chambers with his left hand. He was trying to describe how a body actually works.

Ten years before that, around 1508, he was writing about water. He studied how a river swells in flood, how it digs under a bank, and how it coils into eddies, drawing each shape in careful lines. He wanted one book that explained the movement of water across the earth and in the human body, and he never completed it.

Fourteen years earlier, in 1505, he had written a small notebook on the flight of birds. He watched them turn into the wind and hold a position over the rooftops of Florence, and he drew wings in section with notes on balance and lift. The observations fed straight into his designs for a flying machine.

In 1505 he was also at work on a great wall painting of a cavalry battle for the council chamber of the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence. He tried a new method on dry plaster so that he could work slowly, and the paint began to run down the wall before he had finished. He abandoned the panel.

A year earlier, in 1503, the government of Florence had asked him to design a way to divert the Arno river away from Pisa, which was then under enemy control. He surveyed the valley, drew maps of the channel and the locks, and began work. The scheme was abandoned after a season, and the ground he had opened was left as he found it.

From 1503 he had begun the portrait of a Florentine woman that is now called the Mona Lisa. It is generally identified as the wife of a silk merchant, though the identification is debated. He carried the panel with him for years and kept working on thin translucent layers, which is one reason the surface looks so soft.

Three years earlier, in 1502, he had travelled through central Italy as chief engineer to a military commander, drawing a surveyed map of the town of Imola from measurements he took on the ground. He sketched lock gates, a self-supporting bridge, and covered carts for an eastern sultan. His employer's campaigns moved on, and so did he.

Twice in a lifetime of moving, in 1500 he had returned to Florence because the French army took Milan in December 1499. He had spent seventeen years in Milan as a court artist, and the Sforza family he served was driven out. He travelled north through Mantua and Venice before turning south to a city where his father still worked.

Before that, in 1499, the fate of his great bronze horse was settled by soldiers. The clay model stood in a Milan courtyard and the seven tonnes of metal he had reserved for it had been turned into cannon two years earlier. When French troops occupied the city, their archers used the model for target practice, and it was destroyed.

Four years earlier, between 1495 and 1499, he had painted the Last Supper on the wall of a refectory in Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. He worked slowly on a dry wall with an oil based paint instead of fast fresco, and within a few years the surface was flaking away. He never returned to restore it.

In 1498 he had decorated a room in the Sforza castle in Milan with painted ropes, knots and plants twisting across the ceiling and walls. The design called for the wood paneling to open like a garden. Two years after that, when troops took the city, the room was put to other use and the illusion wore away.

His years in Milan were not only paintings. He designed pageants, costumes, moving scenery and machinery for court celebrations, and he offered plans for canals and dredging on the rivers around the city. He kept a large workshop, took paying pupils, and wrote to his patron almost every year asking for money to finish the bronze horse.

In 1493 he had finally completed the clay model of that horse, more than seven metres high, and it was shown in the city. He had promised a bronze rider more than any European foundry had ever cast. The metal was set aside for other purposes, and the model waited in the courtyard until the soldiers came.

Seven years earlier, around 1490, he had drawn a man inside a circle and a square, working from the measurements of the Roman writer Vitruvius. The sheet is about the proportions of the human body, but it is also an argument that a well built building and a well built person follow the same rules.

In the same period a boy of ten named Gian Giacomo Caprotti arrived in the household and was given the nickname Salai. He remained for almost thirty years, receiving wages, damaging clothes, and living inside the workshop. Leonardo set him to grinding pigments and mixing paint, and he appears in notebooks and pictures across three decades.

A year earlier, in 1489, he had asked for two human skulls so that he could compare them. He drew them in sections, cut through the jaw and the cranium, and argued with himself about where the soul sits and how the optic nerve reaches the eye. His questions were open, and his answers were drawn rather than proved.

Twenty years earlier, around 1482, he had left Florence for Milan with a letter to the local ruler. In it he offered bridges, roads, mines, chariots, covered wagons and cannon, and only at the end did he mention that he could also paint and sculpt. The ruler took him on, and he stayed for seventeen years.

Twenty-one years earlier, in 1481, he had taken a commission from a monastery outside Florence for a large Adoration scene. He laid in the crowd, the ruined steps and the twisted trees, then stopped. The panel was still unfinished when he left the city for Milan, and it was later completed by another painter.

In the mid 1470s he painted a small portrait of a young Florentine woman with a juniper bush behind her head. The panel is crackled and the background has darkened, but the construction of the face is careful and calm. It is one of the earliest works that art historians will assign to his own hand rather than his master's.

In August 1473 he made a drawing of a river valley with hills, a bridge and a town, dated in his own hand. It is the earliest dated sheet we have from him. The lines carry watercourses across rock and the fields break into strokes, and there is no religious subject anywhere on the page.

A year before that, in 1472, he was accepted into the painters' guild of Florence, which meant he could take commissions of his own. The writer Vasari, born a generation later, says an angel that he painted in his master's Baptism of Christ was so fine that the master put down his brush. Vasari's story is a legend as much as a record.

From 1466, at about fourteen, he had been apprenticed in the Florence workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio, a sculptor and painter whose clients included the ruling family. He learned to grind colour, to model clay, to cast metal and to draw the cloth on a live model. Other young men worked at the same benches, and the shop was noisy and full of tests.

Before all of that, he grew up in the Tuscan hill town of Vinci, on the slopes above the Arno, where the wind moves through olive and oak. He was not sent to the classical school where Latin and Greek were taught, and later in life he described himself as a man without letters, proud of what he had taught himself.

He was born on April 15, 1452, in the countryside near the town of Vinci, in the territory of Florence. His father was Ser Piero da Vinci, a Florentine notary, and his mother was a woman named Caterina. He was born out of marriage, which shaped his schooling, and he was left handed, and he wrote backwards.
